newsitem.title: USA: Clinton urges support for Bosnia, Zaire missions.
newsitem.headline: Clinton urges support for Bosnia, Zaire missions.

text.p: President Bill Clinton, calling America the world's "indispensable nation," on Saturday said he approved plans to send U.S. troops to Bosnia and Rwanda after assurances their risks will be limited.

Resting briefly in Hawaii before departing on Monday on a trip to Australia, the Philippines and Thailand, Clinton used his weekly radio address to stress the nation's duties and interests on the world stage.
"As I've said many times, America is the world's indispensable nation, the one the world looks to for leadership because of our strength and our values," he said.
He said the problems in Bosnia and Rwanda "are part of America's responsibilities in the world" and noted Americans must "be ready to share our strength when our values and our interests demand it."
"I've set out clear conditions for American participation to minimize risk and give our troops the best possible chance to make a difference," Clinton said.

On Friday, before leaving on his 12-day trip, Clinton announced that he had agreed to commit 8,500 U.S. ground troops to participate in a new NATO mission aimed at fostering the peace accords in Bosnia.
The current peacekeeping mission, which has involved about 20,000 U.S. forces in Bosnia for the past year, will be withdrawn. Clinton said the "new mission is clear, is limited, and is achievable."
"Its focus should be preventing a renewal of fighting so that reconstruction and reconciliation can accelerate," Clinton said.

In Zaire, where an estimated one million refugees from Rwanda face starvation and death because of renewed fighting among rival factions, Clinton said that "as the world's most powerful nation, we cannot turn our back when so many people, especially so many innocent children, are at mortal risk."

Although he has approved U.S. participation in the mission to Zaire in principle, Clinton has demanded that certain conditions be met -- including having American forces led by a U.S. commander even though the overall operation will be under Canadian command.
Washington also has been pushing for assurances from the warring factions that the rescue mission will not come under direct attack.
"As Zaire and Bosnia remind us, differences among people can fuel the most vicious and violent hatreds," Clinton said, warning that it only leads to "tragedy and despair."
"Let us be ready to share our strength when our values and our interests demand it, with others around the world who need a hand to help themselves to reach their dreams," Clinton said.

Clinton hoped to get some rest in Hawaii, telling reporters on Air Force One en route to Honolulu that he has been up late every night since the Nov. 5 election, in which he won a second four-year term.
He said he had been working on the Bosnia and Rwanda missions and the changes he plans to make in his White House staff and Cabinet when he starts his second term in January.

Clinton is scheduled to make state visits to Australia and Thailand and will attend the fourth annual meeting of the leaders of the 18-nation Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, held this year in the Philippines.
He returns to Washington on Nov. 27, the day before the Thanksgiving holiday.
